newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua C.Bank cautious on reducing devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua C.Bank cautious on reducing devaluation.

text.p: Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman's goal of reducing the devaluation of the cordoba currency must wait until after at least six months of lower inflation, Nicaragua's Central Bank president said on Thursday.

Aleman said on Wednesday that Nicaragua would reduce the rate of devaluation of the government-controlled currency to eight percent a year from the current 12 percent, but did not say when any new policy would be implemented.
In an interview with Reuters, Central Bank President Noel Ramirez appeared to be far more cautious, saying the country needed first to see a "substantial change" in the economy.
"By substantial change I meean that for a relatively long period, from six months to a year, inflation is reduced significantly," Ramirez said.

In addition to lower inflation, Ramirez said he is waiting to see a "significant reduction" in the fiscal deficit, "strong growth" in exports and continued economic aid from friendly foreign governments.
If all goes well in those four areas, "the Central Bank will consider the possibility of gradually reducing the level of devaluation," Ramirez said.

Under the current policy, started under former President Violeta Chamorro, the government devalues the cordoba against the U.S. dollar by a fraction of a cent each day until it adds up to one percent of the cordoba's value per month, or 12 percent a year.
But Nicaraguan inflation is at its lowest level in years, and economic analysts have said the government could be well poised to reduce the devaluations.

"There are positive signs," Eduardo Estrado, editor of the independent financial weekly Mundo Financiero, told Reuters. "Inflation is extremely low, and it's possible that it stays that way and ends around six or seven percent for the year."
Accumulated inflation for the first five months of 1997 was 1.11 percent compared to 5.27 percent for the same period a year ago and a far cry from the five-digit hyperinflation of the late 1980s.
